sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: These are the three things you will be able to do by the end of the lesson.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: An adjective before a noun needs an ending that matches the article, gender and case.

blocks.text: After a definite article, adjectives take a small set of endings. In the nominative, masculine and neuter nouns take -e (der neue Film, das kleine Haus), while feminine and plural nouns take -e as well (die kleine Wohnung, die freundlichen Kollegen).

In the accusative, only the masculine form changes: den neuen Film. After ein-words, the adjective often carries the ending that would otherwise be missing: ein neuer Film, eine kleine Wohnung, ein kleines Haus.

blocks.title: Learn the article and adjective together
blocks.text: Do not memorise endings in isolation. Learn chunks such as der neue Film and den neuen Film as pairs.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

items: After der/die/das, most adjectives take -e or -en.
After ein/eine, the adjective often shows the gender: ein neuer Film.
Adjectives after sein take no ending: Der Film ist neu.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

items.hint: The -e in neue is a clear, short schwa: NOY-e.
The ie in klein is like “ee”: KLINE-e.
The ü is rounded; the -ig ending sounds like -ikh.

blocks.text: Flat-hunting in Germany means reading many short descriptions full of adjective endings: “helle 2-Zimmer-Wohnung”, “ruhige Lage”, “günstige Miete”. Recognising the endings helps you scan listings quickly.
In reviews, adjectives carry the opinion: “ein spannender Film”, “eine langweilige Handlung”. German reviewers often use a noun phrase rather than a full sentence, so the adjective ending matters.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Adjective endings after articles
sections.lede: The article carries the case; the adjective agrees with it.

blocks.text: After sein, adjectives do not take endings: Der Film ist neu. Endings appear only when the adjective stands before a noun.

sections.tip: For the accusative masculine, remember the pair den neuen. The other forms keep -e in the singular.

sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Describe your home or a place you know with three adjective + noun phrases.

model.de: Ich habe eine kleine Wohnung. Die helle Küche ist neu. Der große Balkon ist mein Lieblingsort.
model.en: I have a small flat. The bright kitchen is new. The large balcony is my favourite place.

tips: Use die + -e for feminine nouns and der + -e for masculine subjects.
Use den + -en when the masculine noun is a direct object.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.why: The masculine accusative article is den and the adjective takes -en.
The adjective needs the ending -e after die.
After sein, adjectives do not take comparative endings unless you are actually comparing.
